chunks.title: Optic nerve disease: signs, swelling, atrophy
chunks.tldr: Optic neuropathy = ↓VA, field defect, RAPD, poor colour, disc change. Disc swelling: papillitis, AION, papilloedema (raised ICP), orbital compression, CRVO, hypotony, uveitis. Macular star with disc swelling ('neuroretinitis') — classic Bartonella. Optic atrophy is non-specific; compressive neuropathy may have a normal disc despite bad vision. Hereditary/toxic → temporal pallor (papillomacular bundle). Cupping usually = glaucoma.
chunks.hook: Bad vision + RAPD + normal disc = compress until proven otherwise → image.

cards.q: Which optic neuropathy can show a normal disc despite severe visual loss?
cards.a: Compressive optic neuropathy (and retrobulbar neuritis acutely).

chunks.title: Typical optic neuritis & MS
chunks.tldr: Women 3:1, age 20–40, unilateral; VA falls over 2–7 days, pain on eye movement (90%), RAPD, colour loss; disc normal in ⅔ (retrobulbar). Spontaneous recovery from ~2 wk; >90% ≥6/12 at 1 and 15 y. Steroids (IV methylpred 1 g ×3 d) speed recovery, not final VA (ONTT; oral prednisolone alone ↑ recurrence). MRI brain stratifies MS risk (~50% at 15 y overall). Uhthoff: worse with heat. MS eye signs: optic neuritis (90% at some point), bilateral INO, nystagmus, periphlebitis, intermediate uveitis. Disease-modifying drugs cut relapses. ADEM: kids, post-viral/vaccine, bilateral ON, usually monophasic.
points: Kids: often bilateral, swollen discs, parainfectious.
chunks.hook: Young woman, painful eye movement, slowly dim vision, recovers = demyelinating optic neuritis.

cards.q: What did the ONTT show about IV methylprednisolone?
cards.a: It speeds visual recovery (and short-term reduced MS conversion) but does not change final visual acuity; oral prednisolone alone increased recurrence.

cards.q: What is the Uhthoff phenomenon?
cards.a: Transient worsening of vision (or other MS symptoms) with raised body temperature, e.g. exercise or hot bath.

chunks.title: Atypical optic neuritis: NMO & MOG
chunks.tldr: Red flags: severe pain, NPL, bilateral/simultaneous, worsening >2 wk, no recovery by 6 wk, disc exudates. Work-up: MRI orbits/brain (chiasm involvement → NMO), LP, sarcoid/autoimmune/infection screen, AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG. NMO (Devic): optic neuritis + long transverse myelitis, anti-aquaporin-4, severe disability. MOG: relapsing bilateral ON, ADEM. Rx: IV methylpred → oral pred 1 mg/kg, plasma exchange if poor response, then long-term immunosuppression (anti-B-cell). Others: sarcoid, CRION, SLE, syphilis, TB, Lyme, cat-scratch.
chunks.hook: Optic neuritis that doesn't get better = it isn't typical. Check AQP4 & MOG.

cards.q: Antibody in neuromyelitis optica?
cards.a: Anti-aquaporin-4 IgG (AQP4-IgG).

chunks.title: Ischaemic optic neuropathy
chunks.tldr: NAION: 50s–70s, sudden painless loss (often on waking), inferior altitudinal defect, swollen disc with splinter haems; risk: crowded 'disc at risk', OSA, nocturnal hypotension, DM/HTN, PDE5 inhibitors; 15% fellow eye; ~40% improve; no proven Rx (aspirin for fellow eye?). Arteritic (GCA): >50, severe loss, chalky white swollen disc; also CRAO, cilioretinal occlusion, CWS; headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR, weight loss. ↑ESR/CRP; temporal artery biopsy within 2 wk of steroids (skip lesions; US/PET help). Start steroids immediately: pred 1–1.5 mg/kg or IV methylpred 0.5–1 g ×3 d if bilateral/progressing; taper over 9–12+ months. PION: no disc swelling — blood loss, spine surgery prone, GCA, radiation.
chunks.hook: Over 50 + sudden vision loss → ESR/CRP and ask about the jaw. Treat before biopsy.

cards.q: Disc appearance of arteritic vs non-arteritic AION?
cards.a: Arteritic: pale (chalky white) swelling; NAION: hyperaemic/sectoral swelling with a small crowded fellow disc.

cards.q: Typical field defect in NAION?
cards.a: Inferior altitudinal defect.

chunks.title: Papilloedema & IIH
chunks.tldr: Papilloedema = disc swelling from raised ICP (needs patent nerve sheath). Signs: blurred margins (superior/inferior first), hyperaemia, dilated capillaries, absent SVP, Paton lines; acute → haemorrhages, CWS; chronic → champagne-cork; atrophic late. Takes 1–5 days to appear, 6–8 wk to resolve. Vision usually normal (enlarged blind spot, transient obscurations) until late field constriction. Causes: mass, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis. IIH: obese young women; normal imaging (empty sella, flattened globes) and CSF contents; exclude tetracyclines, vitamin A/retinoids, steroid withdrawal, OSA (men). Rx: weight loss, acetazolamide (250 mg–1 g qds), furosemide; failing vision → optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunt; serial fields.
points: Foster Kennedy: papilloedema one eye + atrophy other (frontal meningioma); pseudo-Foster Kennedy = sequential NAION.
Mimics: buried drusen, small hyperopic discs, myelinated fibres.
chunks.hook: Fat, female, fertile, headache + papilloedema → IIH (after scan + venogram).

cards.q: Drugs associated with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
cards.a: Tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline), vitamin A/retinoids, steroid withdrawal (also lithium, growth hormone).

cards.q: Surgery for IIH with progressive visual loss?
cards.a: Optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting (VP/LP).

chunks.title: Compressive, toxic, traumatic & hereditary optic neuropathy
chunks.tldr: Compression: sphenoid wing/suprasellar/olfactory meningioma, pituitary, craniopharyngioma, aneurysm, TED; optic nerve sheath meningioma (middle-aged women, pale swollen disc + optociliary shunts, 'tram-track' on CT) → stereotactic RT. Nutritional/toxic: bilateral, centrocaecal scotoma, poor colour, temporal pallor — B12/B1/folate, tobacco-alcohol, ethambutol, isoniazid, linezolid, amiodarone (bilateral mild swelling), quinine; methanol (peripapillary oedema; bicarbonate, ethanol/fomepizole, dialysis). Trauma: indirect (forehead blow), avulsion; steroids/decompression unproven. LHON: young men, sequential painless loss, telangiectatic disc that doesn't leak; mtDNA 11778 (commonest), 14484 (best recovery), 3460; avoid smoking/alcohol; idebenone. Dominant optic atrophy (OPA1): childhood insidious, temporal pallor. Wolfram (DIDMOAD).
chunks.hook: Young man, one eye then the other, swollen-looking disc that doesn't leak = LHON.

cards.q: Typical field defect in toxic/nutritional optic neuropathy?
cards.a: Bilateral centrocaecal scotoma.

cards.q: LHON mutation with the best visual prognosis?

chunks.title: Congenital disc anomalies & drusen
chunks.tldr: Hypoplasia: small disc, double-ring sign; septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier) — absent septum pellucidum/corpus callosum + pituitary deficiency (GH). Superior segmental hypoplasia ('topless disc'): mother with type 1 diabetes, inferior field loss. Coloboma (CHARGE, Aicardi with lacunae), morning glory, optic pit (serous macular detachment later), tilted discs (superotemporal field defects mimic chiasm), megalopapilla, myelinated nerve fibres, Bergmeister papilla. Disc drusen: buried in children → pseudopapilloedema (small cupless disc); exposed later, autofluorescent; diagnose with US/CT/OCT; can cause field loss.
chunks.hook: Small disc in a short child = check growth hormone (septo-optic dysplasia).

cards.q: Best test to confirm buried optic disc drusen?
cards.a: B-scan ultrasound (hyperreflective calcification) — also CT, OCT/autofluorescence.

chunks.title: Chiasm & retrochiasmal lesions
chunks.tldr: Chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia, acuity kept until late. Pituitary adenoma: below → upper temporal first; prolactinoma → cabergoline/bromocriptine; others transsphenoidal surgery ± RT; fields recover after decompression (atrophy = poor sign); pituitary apoplexy emergency. Craniopharyngioma (Rathke pouch): kids 10–25 & elderly; from above → lower temporal first; calcified; papilloedema commoner. Suprasellar meningioma (women), chiasmal glioma (NF1). Retrochiasmal → contralateral homonymous: tract (incongruous, contralateral RAPD, bow-tie atrophy), temporal → superior 'pie in the sky', parietal → inferior 'pie on the floor' + OKN asymmetry, occipital → congruous, macular sparing (PCA stroke; >80% of isolated homonymous loss in >50s). Cogan sign: occipital field defect + OKN asymmetry = tumour. PRES (eclampsia, ciclosporin).

cards.q: Field defect from a temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) lesion?
cards.a: Contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

cards.q: Why does a pituitary adenoma typically cause upper temporal loss first?
cards.a: It compresses the chiasm from below, hitting inferonasal crossing fibres (which serve the superotemporal field).

chunks.title: Pupil pathways, RAPD & light-near dissociation
chunks.tldr: Light reflex: retina (incl. ipRGCs) → optic nerve → chiasm → tract → brachium of superior colliculus → pretectal nuclei → both Edinger-Westphal → III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves → sphincter. Normal pupil 3–4 mm; physiological anisocoria (<1 mm) in 30%. RAPD (swinging torch): optic nerve or extensive retina/macula; not from cataract, refractive error, amblyopia (mild at most) or functional loss. Light-near dissociation: afferent defect, Adie, Argyll Robertson (small, irregular, syphilis), Parinaud, diabetes, alcohol.

cards.q: Causes of light-near dissociation?
cards.a: Severe afferent defect, tonic (Adie) pupil, Argyll Robertson pupils, dorsal midbrain syndrome, diabetes/alcoholic neuropathy.

chunks.title: Adie pupil & Horner syndrome
chunks.tldr: Tonic (Adie) pupil: young women; dilated → later small; sectoral sphincter palsy (vermiform), light-near dissociation, slow redilation; supersensitive to 0.1% pilocarpine; ciliary ganglion damage (near fibres 30:1 regrow); ± absent reflexes (Holmes-Adie); 50% other eye in 10 y. Horner: ptosis (Müller), miosis (worse in dim light — dilation lag), ± anhidrosis (central/preganglionic), iris hypochromia if congenital. 1st order: Wallenberg, syrinx; 2nd: Pancoast, neck/thyroid surgery, cervical rib; 3rd: carotid dissection (painful, acute → urgent CTA/MRA), cluster headache, cavernous sinus. Confirm with apraclonidine (reversal of anisocoria) or cocaine; hydroxyamphetamine localises post-ganglionic. Child with acquired Horner → image for neuroblastoma.
chunks.hook: Painful new Horner = carotid dissection until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Apraclonidine test result in Horner syndrome?
cards.a: Reversal of anisocoria — the Horner pupil dilates (denervation supersensitivity) and lid elevates.

cards.q: Pharmacological test for Adie pupil?
cards.a: Constriction to dilute (0.1%) pilocarpine from denervation supersensitivity.

chunks.title: Supranuclear & internuclear disorders
chunks.tldr: Horizontal saccade generator = PPRF (pons); vertical/torsional = riMLF (midbrain); integrators: NPH (horizontal), INC (vertical). Frontal eye field lesion → eyes deviate toward lesion (seizure → away). Pursuit: parieto-occipital, ipsilateral. Parinaud (dorsal midbrain): up-gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation, lid retraction (Collier) — pinealoma, hydrocephalus. INO (MLF): ipsilateral adduction lag + abducting nystagmus of the other eye, convergence spared; young bilateral = MS; elderly = stroke; WEBINO. One-and-a-half: PPRF/VI nucleus + MLF → only abduction of the other eye remains. Convergence insufficiency/spasm of near reflex (functional → miosis + accommodative spasm).
points: VI nucleus lesion = ipsilateral gaze palsy (all movements); PPRF lesion spares vestibular (doll's head).
chunks.hook: INO is named for the eye that can't adduct.

cards.q: Features of right INO?
cards.a: Impaired adduction of the right eye on left gaze, abducting nystagmus of the left eye, convergence preserved.

cards.q: Four signs of Parinaud syndrome?
cards.a: Upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation, eyelid retraction (Collier sign).

chunks.title: Third nerve palsy
chunks.tldr: Nucleus: single central levator subnucleus (→ bilateral ptosis), SR subnuclei innervate contralateral SR. Peripheral palsy: eye down and out, ptosis, ± dilated pupil, no accommodation; SO intorsion still visible. Causes: microvascular (DM/HTN — pupil spared in most; recover by ~3–4 months), PCoA aneurysm (pupil involved, painful → emergency CTA/MRA), trauma, tumour, uncal herniation (fixed dilated pupil), basilar aneurysm (bilateral). Superior division → ptosis + SR. Kids: congenital, ophthalmoplegic migraine, post-viral. Aberrant regeneration (lid lifts on adduction/down-gaze, pupil constricts on adduction) after trauma/aneurysm — never ischaemic; primary aberrant regeneration → cavernous sinus mass. Marcus Gunn jaw-wink (V → levator).
chunks.hook: Painful III with a blown pupil = aneurysm until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Why is the pupil usually spared in microvascular III palsy?
cards.a: Pupillomotor fibres run superficially on the nerve (supplied by pial vessels) and are spared by central ischaemia but hit early by compression.

cards.q: Is aberrant regeneration seen after microvascular III palsy?
cards.a: No — it suggests trauma or compression (aneurysm/tumour).

chunks.title: Fourth & sixth nerve palsies
chunks.tldr: IV: only crossed, dorsal-exiting nerve; longest intracranial course; trauma commonest acquired (bilateral → chin-down, large excyclotorsion, V-pattern); also microvascular, posterior fossa. Hypertropia worse on contralateral gaze and ipsilateral tilt; head tilts away. Congenital: no torsional symptoms, large vertical fusion range, old photos with tilt. SO myokymia: monocular torsional oscillopsia → carbamazepine/β-blocker drops. VI: commonest isolated palsy; long course over petrous apex → false-localising in raised ICP, also low CSF pressure (post-LP), tumour, MS, Chiari; kids → pontine glioma if no trauma. Gradenigo: VI + facial pain + otitis (petrous apex). Mimics: Duane, Möbius, TED, MG, medial wall fracture, convergence spasm. Ischaemic palsies recover by 4 months — otherwise investigate; young or multiple nerves → urgent imaging.
points: Cavernous sinus/SOF/apex syndromes combine III, IV, VI (+V, + II at apex). Sudden total ophthalmoplegia: brainstem stroke, Wernicke, Miller Fisher, pituitary apoplexy, botulism, MG crisis.
chunks.hook: VI palsy in a child without trauma → MRI the pons.

cards.q: What is Gradenigo syndrome?
cards.a: Abducens palsy + ipsilateral facial pain (V) + otorrhoea from petrous apicitis (complicated otitis media).

cards.q: How long to wait for a presumed microvascular cranial nerve palsy to recover before imaging?
cards.a: About 3–4 months; no recovery → investigate.

chunks.title: Myasthenia gravis & CPEO
chunks.tldr: MG: fatigable ptosis/diplopia, worse in evening, no pupil involvement, can mimic any palsy/INO. ⅓ start ocular; ⅔ of those generalise (mostly within 1 y). Associations: thymoma 15%, thyroid disease, autoimmunity; drugs worsen (β-blockers, aminoglycosides, statins, penicillamine, quinine). Tests: AChR antibodies (80–90% generalised, 40–60% ocular), MuSK, ice-pack test, rest test, edrophonium (with atropine), repetitive stimulation, single-fibre EMG (orbicularis); CT chest. Rx: pyridostigmine (ocular responds less), steroids, azathioprine, IVIG/plasma exchange, thymectomy. CPEO: slow symmetric ptosis + ophthalmoplegia, no diplopia usually, normal pupils; mtDNA deletion; Kearns-Sayre = CPEO + pigmentary retinopathy + heart block before 15 y (ECG!).
chunks.hook: Variable ptosis that improves with ice = myasthenia.

cards.q: Triad of Kearns-Sayre syndrome?
cards.a: CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy and cardiac conduction block, onset before age 15.

cards.q: Most sensitive test for ocular myasthenia?
cards.a: Single-fibre EMG (e.g. of orbicularis oculi).

chunks.title: Nystagmus types
chunks.tldr: Named by fast phase. Physiological: end-point, OKN (asymmetric horizontal → parietal lesion; useful in functional loss), caloric (COWS). Infantile/congenital: by 6 mo, horizontal even in upgaze, null zone (head turn), damps with convergence, no oscillopsia; look for sensory cause (albinism, aniridia, achromatopsia, ONH, LCA). Latent: with infantile ET, beats toward fixing eye on occlusion. Spasmus nutans: nodding + head tilt + fine asymmetric nystagmus, resolves — exclude chiasmal glioma. Peripheral vestibular: horizontal-torsional, beats away from lesion, suppressed by fixation, vertigo/tinnitus. Downbeat: cervicomedullary junction (Chiari), cerebellar, lithium, anticonvulsants. Upbeat: brainstem, drugs. Gaze-evoked: cerebellum/drugs; Bruns (CPA). See-saw: chiasm/parasellar. Convergence-retraction: Parinaud. PAN: cerebellar, baclofen. Oculopalatal tremor after brainstem stroke.
points: Mimics: square-wave jerks, opsoclonus (neuroblastoma in kids), ocular flutter, voluntary nystagmus.
chunks.hook: Downbeat = Down at the foramen magnum (Chiari) — get an MRI.

cards.q: Localisation of downbeat nystagmus?
cards.a: Cervicomedullary junction/cerebellum (e.g. Arnold-Chiari malformation); also drugs (lithium, anticonvulsants).

cards.q: COWS mnemonic for calorics?
cards.a: Cold water → fast phase Opposite; Warm → Same side.

chunks.title: Transient visual loss, stroke & migraine
chunks.tldr: Amaurosis fugax: monocular curtain 5–10 min — retinal emboli (carotid, cardiac): Hollenhorst cholesterol (glinting, bifurcations), platelet-fibrin (white, transient), calcific (valves, CRAO). Treat as TIA: aspirin, BP/lipids, carotid Doppler, endarterectomy for 70–99% stenosis. Also GCA, hyperviscosity, antiphospholipid. Ocular ischaemic syndrome: mid-peripheral blot haemorrhages, dilated non-tortuous veins, NVI, anterior uveitis — severe carotid disease. Vertebrobasilar: bilateral greying. PCA occlusion: homonymous (superior) field loss, alexia without agraphia. Subdural: ipsilateral dilated pupil = herniation. SAH: thunderclap, Terson. Migraine aura: bilateral homonymous fortification spectrum expanding over 15–30 min.
chunks.hook: Amaurosis fugax = a TIA of the eye — same-day stroke work-up.

cards.q: What are Hollenhorst plaques?
cards.a: Refractile cholesterol emboli at retinal arteriolar bifurcations, usually from carotid atheroma.

cards.q: Retinal signs of ocular ischaemic syndrome?
cards.a: Mid-peripheral dot-blot haemorrhages, dilated non-tortuous veins, narrowed arteries, NVD/NVI; often low IOP with anterior segment inflammation.

chunks.title: Phakomatoses
chunks.tldr: NF1 (17q, 1:3000): ≥6 café-au-lait, neurofibromas, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules (~93%), plexiform lid neurofibroma, optic pathway glioma (bilateral ON glioma pathognomonic), sphenoid dysplasia, congenital glaucoma. NF2 (22q): bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas; PSC cataract in ~75%, ERM, combined hamartoma, ONSM. VHL (3p, AD): retinal capillary haemangioma, cerebellar haemangioblastoma, RCC, phaeo, cysts — lifelong screening. Sturge-Weber (sporadic): port-wine stain (V1/V2), leptomeningeal angioma (seizures, tram-track calcification), ipsilateral glaucoma (lid involvement), diffuse choroidal haemangioma in 40%. Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 chr 9, TSC2 chr 16): adenoma sebaceum, ash-leaf spots, seizures, retinal astrocytoma, renal angiomyolipoma. Ataxia-telangiectasia (AR): conjunctival telangiectasia, ataxia, infections, oculomotor apraxia. Wyburn-Mason: retinal + midbrain AVMs.
chunks.hook: NF1 = 17 letters in 'von Recklinghausen'; NF2 = 22 (two ears, chr 22).

cards.q: Ocular feature present in most NF2 patients?
cards.a: Early posterior subcapsular (or cortical) lens opacities (~75%).

cards.q: Ocular manifestations of Sturge-Weber?
cards.a: Ipsilateral glaucoma, diffuse choroidal haemangioma ('tomato ketchup' fundus), episcleral haemangioma, port-wine stain on lids.
